source.title: Internal Data Repetition Destroys Language Models
source.authors: Jessica Chudnovsky; Joshua Kazdan; Noam Levi; Rylan Schaeffer; Yegor Denisov-Blanch; Bo-Yang He; M. Donmez; O. Koyejo; D. Donoho

page_placements.theme: Repetition and data replay alter generalization

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double descent and reports its own non-monotonic effects of repetition, but it does not test any listed version's size-, epoch-, sample-size-, or capacity-wise double-descent claim.
record.gate_note: The study varies repetition count and repeated-pool concentration at fixed compute and repeated-token fraction. Its loss peaks over repetition settings are related to, but do not measure, the axes named in the claim versions. Rows below record those distinct findings; no cited results from other work are included.
record.test_reason: The study varies how a fixed 10% repeated-token budget is concentrated (repeat count R versus pool size Dr) at fixed compute and fixed total tokens. It reports eval-loss peaks over R, and its toy OLS model shows peaks over repeat count r and pool size d. None of these axes is one the versions name: model size across an interpolation threshold, training epochs, number of training samples, or capacity. Double descent is cited only as related theory. No version is tested, so the reader's T6/discusses holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. To complete it: at fixed f = 0.1 and fixed compute, loss peaks at an intermediate repeat count. The peak location follows Rpeak ∝ N^-0.96, so the most damaging repeated-pool size grows faster than compute. The worst case at 344M, OT = 1 gives CEL ≈ 0.33. A misspecified linear regression with verbatim duplicates reproduces the peak, which the authors read as a generic statistical memorization–generalization tradeoff.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Qwen3-style models with controlled exact document replay at a fixed repeated-token fraction and measures eval loss and compute-equivalent loss; it does not reproduce the original size-, epoch-, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that overtraining multiplier shifts the level of CEG but leaves the peak location in R approximately unchanged; peak sharpness varies between sweeps. The larger-model sweep grid is incomplete.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed compute and f = 0.1, eval loss peaks at intermediate repeat count R, 1.0 to 4.2% above the no-repetition baseline (median 3.1%). The fitted peak follows Rpeak ∝ N^-0.96. A toy misspecified OLS model shows similar non-monotonicity in r and d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed repeated-data token budget, concentrating repetition onto a subset of documents produces an intermediate-concentration peak in held-out loss, located at a point that depends on model size.

fits_no_version.finding: At OT = 1, the worst repetition settings give CEL of 0.19 to 0.33 across the six sizes, 34M to 344M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Worst-case exact document repetition at a 10% token fraction costs about 19 to 33% compute-equivalent loss in small Qwen3-style models, rising with size.

record.problems: The experiments use one Qwen3-style architecture family, one corpus, and a largest model of 344M parameters. Each (N, OT, R) cell is a single training run, with no seed-level variance estimate. The larger-model grid is incomplete. Absolute CEG/CEL values rely on a three-parameter scaling-law fit to six OT = 1 baselines and are presented as point estimates. The toy regression omits features of language models and is explicitly explanatory rather than quantitative.

untested.parts: No test-error sweep over model size; six sizes appear only as separate repetition sweeps.
Only final checkpoints are evaluated; no test-loss curve over training time.
Total tokens are fixed per sweep; there is no increase in sample count near an interpolation threshold.
The toy OLS model is not swept across an interpolation point in capacity m.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs and samples.
No label-noise or regularization sweep; labels are noiseless; no multiple descent.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is about data repetition. It links its toy model to the double-descent and benign-overfitting literature only conceptually. It is a preprint; each cell is a single run and the larger-model grid is incomplete.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error sweep over model size.
No test-error curve over training epochs or time; final checkpoints are evaluated.
No sweep increasing the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
The toy regression varies repetition count and repeated-pool size, not model capacity across an interpolation point.

The paper fits how the repetition-count location of the loss peak varies with model size, but does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
No sweep of label noise or regularization, nor a test of triple or multiple descent.
No test of whether re-counting complexity converts a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Qwen3-style models (completed sweeps, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep per-document repeat count R at fixed compute and repeated-token fraction f = 0.1.

conditions.value: OT ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}, with an incomplete larger-model grid
fixed held-out split of approximately 150M tokens

rows.measure: Maximum eval-loss increase over the corresponding no-repetition baseline across completed sweeps
rows.value: Raw maximum 1.0 to 4.2% above baseline, median 3.1%; peak prominence relative to the larger endpoint ranged from 0.7 to 2.7%, median 1.8%.
rows.note: Aggregate result across completed sweeps; the reported loss peak is over repetition count, not a listed claim axis.

rows.subject: Qwen3-style models (completed sweeps, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit the repeat count at peak eval loss against model size across completed (N, OT) sweeps.
rows.measure: Fitted peak repeat count as a function of parameter count
rows.note: This describes the repetition-count location of the loss peak; it is not a model-size double-descent curve.
rows.check: Link is correct. Model size enters only as a predictor of where the repetition peak sits. It is not a test-error sweep over size, so it does not bear on V1 or V5.

rows.subject: Misspecified linear regression (OLS)
rows.size_stated: Observed dimension m varies; examples include m = 48 and m = 384
rows.operation_detail: Simulate test loss while varying repeated-pool size d and repeat count r at fixed settings of the other quantities.

conditions.value: n unique examples plus d examples each repeated r times
no-repetition baseline at the same m

rows.baseline: No-repetition baseline at the same m
rows.value: Text reports non-monotonic excess test loss in repeated-pool size d at fixed m and r; the peak shifts to larger d as m grows.
rows.uncertainty: Theory and simulation agree to within numerical precision
rows.note: The non-monotonicity is over repeated-pool size and repetition, not capacity across an interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: Misspecified linear regression (OLS)
rows.operation_detail: Vary repeat count r with repeated samples fixed at 10% of the training budget.
rows.measure: Sample efficiency (clean unique-sample budget needed to match repeated-data test loss divided by actual samples)
rows.baseline: Clean unique data; efficiency baseline shown as 1
rows.value: Text reports sample efficiency falls sharply at intermediate r and partially recovers at extreme r.
rows.uncertainty: Theory and simulation shown; no seed-level uncertainty stated
rows.note: This is a sample-efficiency analogue in the toy model, not test error as a function of sample size.
rows.check: Link is correct. The total sample budget is fixed and only the repeat structure varies, so this is not V3's more-samples-can-hurt effect.
